reasoning: 12-year-old with head trauma and loss of consciousness (LOC) for ~30 seconds—even brief LOC after blunt head injury is a red flag for intracranial injury in pediatric patients.
Chief complaint of severe headache + nausea post-head injury raises concern for concussion or intracranial pathology; nausea in this context is particularly worrisome.
Vital signs are age-appropriate and stable (BP 108/72, HR 90, RR 18 all normal for 12-year-old), which is reassuring but does NOT rule out significant head injury.
Pediatric patients can present deceptively well initially despite serious intracranial injury; absence of vomiting and alert mental status do not exclude evolving complications.
No helmet use + direct impact to pavement = mechanism of injury consistent with moderate-to-severe head trauma.
Per ESI criteria, any head injury with LOC and persistent symptoms (headache, nausea) in a child should be considered high-risk and requires urgent evaluation; cannot safely observe at lower acuity.
This patient requires imaging (likely CT head), neurological examination, and close monitoring—meets 'high-risk situation' criterion for ESI-2 even with currently stable vitals.
red_flags: Loss of consciousness (30 seconds) following head trauma
Nausea in the context of head trauma
No helmet protection; direct impact mechanism
Pediatric patient with potential intracranial injury—higher risk for rapid deterioration
Cannot reliably assess for evolving intracranial complications at triage alone
